## Chapter Summary

Internal and external auditors differ in purpose, but they rely more and more on the same analytics. Analytics lets them test every record in a population instead of a sample. Testing a whole population produces exceptions, and most of them are false positives. The auditor's judgment therefore goes into designing each test, investigating each exception, and recording a disposition for it. The work follows a workflow: state the objective, reconcile the population to the ledger, run the tests, investigate the exceptions, record their dispositions, and document the whole in a workpaper.

Reconciling a population's count and total to the general ledger confirms that a test covers every record. Stratification then shows where the value lies. At Charles River, most supplier payments are small, fewer than a thousand payments of $10,000 or more hold about a third of the value, and four payments are large enough to examine one by one. A first-digit test compares the payments' leading digits with Benford's Law, and the mean absolute deviation measures how closely they conform. The payments conform only marginally, and splitting them shows why. Partial payments come only from invoices of $1,000 or more, a subset selected by size, so they do not conform; full payments and the invoices themselves do. A nonconforming digit test points to where to look. It does not show that anything is wrong.

An aging schedule classifies open invoices by days past due at an as-of date. It supports the estimate of the allowance for credit losses, which the credit loss standard of the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB) requires even when the risk of loss is remote. Charles River's customers pay mostly on time. The reconciliation of the aged invoices to the accounts receivable account, however, found a round difference: an opening balance, recorded in the first journal entry, that no invoice supports and no receipt has reduced. The company has also never recorded an allowance. Confirmations provide external evidence of the balances. The auditor confirms the largest balances in full and a random sample of the rest, and freezes the selection with Paste Values so that it can be reviewed.

Journal entry testing looks for the characteristics that auditing standards associate with fraudulent entries. Examples are entries recorded after the period they affect, entries by people who do not usually make them, and round amounts, together with tests of approval. Flags for each characteristic add up to a risk score that ranks entries for review. Some flagged patterns have ordinary explanations, such as month-end depreciation on a weekend. Others, such as entries approved by their own creators, point to weaknesses in the approval controls. The highest-scoring entry was the opening balance entry, the same entry that the receivables reconciliation had found. Duplicate, near-duplicate, gap, and threshold tests complete the auditor's toolkit. A workpaper that records the population, parameters, exceptions, dispositions, and conclusion of each test makes the analytics reviewable and repeatable.
